title: Saaty school selection example (three high schools, six criteria)
description: One of the earliest published AHP applications: Saaty's family ranked three high schools against six characteristics (Saaty 1977, pp. 265-266). The matrices in this fixture were verified entry-by-entry against the original paper (Table 10 and the six school comparison matrices), and the paper's published results - the criteria eigenvector (0.32, 0.14, 0.03, 0.13, 0.24, 0.14), the Table 11 school eigenvectors and eigenvalues, and the final priorities A = 0.37, B = 0.38, C = 0.25 - are recorded in source_reported, where their agreement with the derived values is stated. Expected values are derived at six decimals because the paper publishes at two. The criteria matrix is a well-known example of a strongly inconsistent judgment matrix (lambda_max 7.42 for n = 6; CR about 0.23 under Saaty's RI; the paper notes the inconsistency and that no revision was made). Note also that on this example the final ranking of schools A and B differs between the principal-eigenvector synthesis (B slightly ahead of A) and the column-normalization approximation (A slightly ahead of B) - see the synthesis alternate; the margin is about 0.01 either way, so implementations using different documented prioritization methods can legitimately report different top choices on this fixture.

source.citation: T. L. Saaty, 'A scaling method for priorities in hierarchical structures', Journal of Mathematical Psychology 15(3), 1977, pp. 234-281; the school selection example, Table 10 and the school comparison matrices, pp. 265-266.
source.notes: Matrices verified against the original paper. They are also reproduced in N. Krivulin, 'Tropical implementation of the analytical hierarchy process decision method', arXiv:1802.01989, Section 5.2, which is a convenient open-access copy.

scale.name: saaty-1-9
scale.notes: Judgments on Saaty's fundamental 1-9 scale; reciprocals (e.g. 1/3) and intermediate or fractional values are valid entries. Matrix entries may be given as numbers or as fraction strings such as "1/3".

stability.description: The Percent-Top question of Triantaphyllou and Sanchez (1997) applied to this hierarchy's criterion weights: for each criterion, the smallest relative change to its weight (in percent of the weight; negative = decrease) that makes a different alternative rank first. At the baseline School B ranks first, and in every feasible case the displacing alternative is School A. Two documented conventions are given. 'theorem-1' (the normative block) changes only the selected weight, per the paper's Theorem 1, with the feasibility condition that the new weight stays in [0, 1]. The 'proportional-redistribution' alternate also rescales the remaining weights so the sum stays 1 - the convention of interactive AHP sensitivity tools; a tool is checked against the block matching its documented convention, and divergence between the blocks is a convention difference, not an error. All values are derived from this fixture's derived principal-eigenvector criteria weights and local priorities, and recompute via tools/compute_expected.py. A null entry means no feasible change to that criterion's weight displaces the top alternative: the Friends matrix rates the three schools equally, so under theorem-1 no crossing exists, and under redistribution the scores tie only in the degenerate limit where Friends carries the entire weight.

provenance.method: Theorem 1 of the cited paper applied to the fixture's derived criteria weights and local priorities (only the selected weight changes); smallest-magnitude feasible threshold per criterion.
provenance.citation: E. Triantaphyllou and A. Sanchez, 'A sensitivity analysis approach for some deterministic multi-criteria decision-making methods', Decision Sciences 28(1), 1997, pp. 151-185.

source_reported.explanation: The paper publishes its results at two decimals; the derived values in this fixture agree with every published figure at that rounding, with two typographical exceptions. First, the paper prints the criteria matrix's principal eigenvalue as lambda_max = 7.49, while recomputation from its own Table 10 gives 7.4199 (7.42 at two decimals); the paper's accompanying eigenvector recomputes exactly, so the printed eigenvalue appears to be a typographical slip. Second, Table 11 prints School life's priority for school C as 0.46 where the exact value is 0.4545 (0.45 at plain rounding), consistent with rounding the column to sum to 1.00.
source_reported.citation: T. L. Saaty, 'A scaling method for priorities in hierarchical structures', Journal of Mathematical Psychology 15(3), 1977, pp. 234-281; the school selection example, Table 10 and the school comparison matrices, pp. 265-266. Eigenvector and lambda_max of Table 10 from p. 266; school eigenvectors and eigenvalues from Table 11; final priorities from p. 266.
